title: Cordless Spin Scrubbers for Tubs and Tile: Less Scrubbing Strain, and What to Check First
subtitle: A battery-powered brush on a long handle can lighten the scrubbing in bathroom cleaning, but it helps to know what to check before you buy.
excerpt: If scrubbing the tub leaves your wrists aching and your back sore, a cordless spin scrubber can do the circular motion for you. Here is what these tools can and cannot do, and three models with published prices.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Cleaning a bathtub can mean kneeling on a hard floor, leaning over the tub edge and working a brush in small circles until the wrists complain. Grout lines and the corners of a shower can be even harder on the hands.

A cordless spin scrubber is one way to ease that strain. It is a rechargeable brush on a long handle that spins on its own, so you guide it instead of scrubbing by hand. It will not make a bathroom clean itself, and it is not a cure for pain, but it may make the job less tiring.

Inside the head is a small motor powered by a rechargeable battery that spins the brush. Models come with a set of interchangeable brush heads. For example, the Tilswall page describes wide flat heads for floors and walls, a round head for tubs and sinks, and a pointed head for grout and corners. An extendable handle lets you reach the far side of a tub or the upper part of a shower wall while standing on the floor.

Consumer Reports tested power scrubbers and found that cleaning results were fairly similar from model to model, with battery life the main difference. The article's date is not shown in the copy we could read, and that copy appeared to be partial, so some details may be missing.
"The biggest difference between a good electric power scrubber and a subpar one is actually battery life." — Dan Kahl, Consumer Reports test lead

Be realistic about cleaning power. A Consumer Reports writer noted that a power scrubber can't deep-clean as effectively as a strong person working a brush. Think of it as moderate scrubbing with little strain on you. You will still need a bathroom cleaner for soap scum, mineral deposits and grout; the brush does not replace the cleaner.

items: Battery runtime: look for a stated number of minutes, and expect less if you press down hard, since pressure drains the battery faster. Consumer Reports runtime figures appear to conflict (one copy says over an hour for the shortest-running model, another snapshot says about 10 minutes for two models), so treat runtimes as unsettled and check the live page.

Handle reach: check how far the handle extends and whether it sets to several lengths. None of the three pages below gives a handle length range. Keimi lists seven adjustable lengths, but not the minimum or maximum.
Head design: Consumer Reports counted an adjustable head angle and a handle that pops off for tight spots as useful design points. HOTO's page says its 45° head reduces strain during use.

Water resistance: IPX7 is a general standard that covers temporary immersion, not regular soaking of electronics. HOTO and keimi list IPX7; the Tilswall page lists no water rating. Either way, do not charge near a sink or tub.
Weight and grip: none of the three pages list weight, grip size or trigger type. If your hands are stiff, try one in a store if you can, or ask the seller.
Ongoing costs: the pages showed no subscriptions, but replacement brush head prices and battery replacement policies were not published on any of them. Ask before you buy.
Returns: only keimi's page documents a return window (90 days at The Home Depot). The return terms for Tilswall and HOTO were not confirmed, so check before ordering.

sections.content: Follow the maker's manual for charging, cleaning and care. Set the handle so you can stand upright with your arms comfortable, not stretched out. Spray your cleaner, then let the brush do the work with light pressure, which also helps the battery last longer.

Use the wide head for big surfaces and a pointed head for grout and corners, if your model includes them. If scrubbing causes wrist or back pain, talk with your doctor or a physical therapist about it. A cleaning tool is not a substitute for that advice.

A long handle is there so you never have to climb into the tub to clean it. Stay on the bathroom floor, on a dry nonslip mat if you have one, and keep one hand free to steady yourself. Charge the scrubber on a dry counter away from the sink, tub and shower.
sections.label: Safety First

sections.content: A spin scrubber is not for everyone. If you cannot comfortably hold a handle, need heavy-duty grout cleaning every day, or need a verified runtime for a whole bathroom, it may not suit you. But if you want less strain while keeping the tub clean, it is worth a careful look.

products.price: $49.99 per box (The Home Depot; check current price)
products.blurb: Lists an IPX7 water rating, dual spin speeds, eight brush heads and a handle with seven adjustable lengths, plus a 90-day return window at The Home Depot. Battery capacity, runtime and handle length range are not listed.

products.name: Tilswall Cordless Spin Scrubber (M3)
products.blurb: Comes with four heads covering walls, tubs, sinks and grout, a 4000mAh battery and an adjustable long handle. Runtime, weight, handle length range and water rating are not listed, so ask before ordering.

products.name: HOTO Electric Spin Scrubber
products.blurb: Has a 45-degree angled head that the page says reduces strain during use, two speeds, six interchangeable heads, an extendable handle and an IPX7 rating. Runtime, battery capacity and handle length range are not listed.

products.name: Power Scour Cordless Power Scrubber
products.blurb: A cordless, rechargeable scrubber with interchangeable brush heads that does the scrubbing motion for you, which helps if gripping and pressing is hard on your hands.
